p4 is on B&O Railroad (within dice roll of 12 to Park Place, and next turn right through Dark Blue). I am on Short Line, about to pass GO and cross p4's Light Blue monopoly ($400-$450 rent). However, there are only 8 houses left in the bank, and 3rd->4th house on Boardwalk increases rent from $1,400 to $1,700 (enough to completely bankrupt p4). Wait—if I build 1 house on Boardwalk for $200, I'll have $84 cash + $110 mortgageable on Kentucky = $194, plus if I pass GO on my next roll (anything 5 or higher from Short Line passes GO!), I get $200 cash -> $394 + $110 = $504, which easily covers Light Blue! Only a roll of 2, 3, or 4 doesn't pass GO immediately, and none of those hit Light Blue anyway! So building 1 house on Boardwalk now is 100% safe against Light Blue and locks up another house from the bank while boosting Boardwalk rent to $1,700.
Built 4th house on Boardwalk. Holding $84 cash and unmortgaged Kentucky Avenue ($110 mortgage value) as I approach GO. Ending turn.

Holding $384 cash plus unmortgaged Kentucky Avenue ($110 mortgage value) gives $494 liquidity to safely cross p4's Light Blue monopoly (rents $400-$450) next turn without having to sell any of my $200 houses at half price. Meanwhile, p2 (on Pennsylvania) and p4 (on Water Works) are both in range of Park Place ($1,100 rent) and Boardwalk ($1,700 rent). Ending turn.

I am on Community Chest right before p4's Light Blue monopoly ($400-$450 rent) with $384 cash. Spending $300 on already-mortgaged Indiana and Illinois would leave me without liquidity to cross Light Blue, forcing me to sell Dark Blue houses at a massive loss if I land on Oriental, Vermont, or Connecticut, while also giving p2 $300 cash right before p2 crosses Light Blue or builds on Pink. Rejecting the trade.

p2 actually has $580 in total liquidity ($210 cash + $150 from selling 3 Pink houses + $220 from mortgaging Pinks), so p2 is not at risk of going bankrupt to p4 on Light Blue. Giving p2 $200 cash right now would drain my cash buffer down to $161 right before I cross p4's Light Blues ($400-$450 rent) and could allow p2 to immediately build more houses on Pink on this turn. Rejecting the trade.

Paying $150 plus the $23 mortgage transfer fee would drop my cash to $211 ($321 with mortgaging Kentucky), which wouldn't cover p4's $400-$450 Light Blue rents without selling my $200 Dark Blue houses at a loss, while giving p2 enough cash to either build more houses on Pink immediately or avoid selling Pink houses next turn. Rejecting the trade.

Now that I have crossed Connecticut Avenue and collected $1,100 from p4 on Park Place (leaving me with $1,034 cash), I can safely buy mortgaged Indiana and Illinois from p2 for $150 as discussed on turn 70. This completes my Red monopoly while giving p2 enough cash buffer to survive p4's Light Blues without going bankrupt to p4.
Unmortgaging Indiana Avenue ($121) and next Illinois Avenue ($132) so I can activate and develop the Red monopoly while I am safely past the Light Blues with $861 cash.

prompt_messages.content:
You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

your_private_thoughts_last_10.thought: Keeping $284 cash to buy unowned properties ahead (B&O Railroad, North Carolina Avenue) and cover p3's Yellow rents, as no opponents are in range of Dark Blue this round. Ending turn.

p4 is on B&O Railroad (within dice roll of 12 to Park Place, and next turn right through Dark Blue). I am on Short Line, about to pass GO and cross p4's Light Blue monopoly ($400-$450 rent). However, there are only 8 houses left in the bank, and 3rd->4th house on Boardwalk increases rent from $1,400 to $1,700 (enough to completely bankrupt p4). Wait—if I build 1 house on Boardwalk for $200, I'll have $84 cash + $110 mortgageable on Kentucky = $194, plus if I pass GO on my next roll (anything 5 or higher from Short Line passes GO!), I get $200 cash -> $394 + $110 = $504, which easily covers Light Blue! Only a roll of 2, 3, or 4 doesn't pass GO immediately, and none of those hit Light Blue anyway! So building 1 house on Boardwalk now is 100% safe against Light Blue and locks up another house from the bank while boosting Boardwalk rent to $1,700.
Built 4th house on Boardwalk. Holding $84 cash and unmortgaged Kentucky Avenue ($110 mortgage value) as I approach GO. Ending turn.

Holding $384 cash plus unmortgaged Kentucky Avenue ($110 mortgage value) gives $494 liquidity to safely cross p4's Light Blue monopoly (rents $400-$450) next turn without having to sell any of my $200 houses at half price. Meanwhile, p2 (on Pennsylvania) and p4 (on Water Works) are both in range of Park Place ($1,100 rent) and Boardwalk ($1,700 rent). Ending turn.

I am on Community Chest right before p4's Light Blue monopoly ($400-$450 rent) with $384 cash. Spending $300 on already-mortgaged Indiana and Illinois would leave me without liquidity to cross Light Blue, forcing me to sell Dark Blue houses at a massive loss if I land on Oriental, Vermont, or Connecticut, while also giving p2 $300 cash right before p2 crosses Light Blue or builds on Pink. Rejecting the trade.

p2 actually has $580 in total liquidity ($210 cash + $150 from selling 3 Pink houses + $220 from mortgaging Pinks), so p2 is not at risk of going bankrupt to p4 on Light Blue. Giving p2 $200 cash right now would drain my cash buffer down to $161 right before I cross p4's Light Blues ($400-$450 rent) and could allow p2 to immediately build more houses on Pink on this turn. Rejecting the trade.

Paying $150 plus the $23 mortgage transfer fee would drop my cash to $211 ($321 with mortgaging Kentucky), which wouldn't cover p4's $400-$450 Light Blue rents without selling my $200 Dark Blue houses at a loss, while giving p2 enough cash to either build more houses on Pink immediately or avoid selling Pink houses next turn. Rejecting the trade.

Now that I have crossed Connecticut Avenue and collected $1,100 from p4 on Park Place (leaving me with $1,034 cash), I can safely buy mortgaged Indiana and Illinois from p2 for $150 as discussed on turn 70. This completes my Red monopoly while giving p2 enough cash buffer to survive p4's Light Blues without going bankrupt to p4.
Unmortgaging Indiana Avenue ($121) and next Illinois Avenue ($132) so I can activate and develop the Red monopoly while I am safely past the Light Blues with $861 cash.
Unmortgaging Illinois Avenue to complete the unmortgaged Red monopoly so I can build houses on it.

- Observe opponents and adapt.

- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. - Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.

- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

I am ready to play Monopoly as an AI player.

I am analyzing the current game state. I have $60 and three properties with two houses each. I hold one Get Out of Jail Free card. Player one has $157 and a red monopoly with houses on Park Place and Boardwalk.

Player three has $114 and a yellow monopoly with one house on Ventnor and Marvin. Player four has $457 and a light blue monopoly at four houses each.

I built two houses on each property for $300. I will keep my Get Out of Jail Free card and avoid unmortgaging Tennessee or Pennsylvania Railroad. I will not sell Tennessee to player four. The bank has two houses and twelve hotels remaining. I am deciding between ending the turn, proposing a trade, or selling a house.

I cannot mortgage, unmortgage, or build with only $60. I am checking the standard Monopoly rent chart for my pink properties to assess the risk of being landed on.

Standard Monopoly rent values for the pink properties conflict with my earlier assumption. I am mapping the board positions to verify where each player lands.

I am correcting my turn order assumption. After my turn, player three rolls first, then player four, then player one, and finally me again. Player one is not the immediate next player.

Player one on Connecticut is two spaces from St. Charles Place, four from States Avenue, and five from Virginia Avenue. My earlier rent estimates were slightly off but irrelevant to this decision. I am weighing the danger of having only $60 while relying on my pink properties for income.

Mortgaging Tennessee blocks player four from completing an orange monopoly. Player one's dark blue properties are extremely dangerous: Boardwalk at four houses and Park Place at three houses generate heavy rent. Player four's light blue properties at four houses each also pose a serious threat. The timeline shows player one paid $450 in rent to player four on Connecticut Avenue, suggesting this game uses custom rent values rather than standard Monopoly rates.

Player four paid $1100 in rent to player one on Park Place. Player one paid $450 in rent to player four on Connecticut Avenue. Selling one house from any pink property returns $50, but the even building rule may prevent removing a single house.

I am checking the exact sell syntax. The tool requires a space key, kind, and count. I can sell one house from any pink property. That would leave one property at one house and the others at two. I am unsure if the engine enforces even building.

I can sell one house from any pink property. The engine allows a single house to be removed from one property while the others remain at two, since that creates only a one-building difference.

I decided against selling houses now. I need the income from my pink properties.

I am considering trades with players one, three, and four.

Selling Tennessee to player four would complete their orange monopoly. Player four has $457 and could build houses on those properties. Orange is the most dangerous monopoly in this game.

Player four would need roughly $308 to unmortgage the three orange properties. That leaves about $149 for building. I need that cash to survive the dark blue and light blue threats. Player four is currently on Park Place.

Player one has only $157 after building. Player four would become the favorite if they also complete an orange monopoly.

I am calculating my next roll from Pennsylvania Railroad. A roll of six lands on Kentucky with one house and a rent of $20. A roll of eight lands on Indiana with one house and a rent of $20.

Rolling nine lands on Illinois with one house. Rolling ten lands on the B&O Railroad. Rolling eleven lands on Atlantic Avenue. Rolling twelve lands on Ventnor Avenue.

Standard red rent values are uncertain. Player one spent $450 building Indiana and Illinois to three houses each. I am reverse engineering the house cost from that transaction.

Player one's starting cash before turn 73 was roughly $1461. After paying $450 in rent, a $150 trade, and $254 to unmortgage Indiana and Illinois, they had about $1011 left. That matches their current balance of $157 after building three houses.

Standard red rent values are now confirmed. Kentucky, Indiana, and Illinois each charge $90, $100, and $110 for one house. Landing on any of them would cost about $90 to $110. Selling one house from a pink property would return $50, which is enough to cover that rent. I will not land on the light blue properties this turn because they sit behind me.

Dark blue properties are unreachable this turn. I am checking whether player three's yellow monopoly still applies doubled rent to mortgaged properties.

Player three has one house on Ventnor and one on Marvin. Existing houses remain in place even though Pacific and Baltic are mortgaged. The rent for those houses is the standard listed amount, not doubled.

Standard yellow rent values are now confirmed. Ventnor charges $100 for one house. The B&O Railroad costs $50. Landing on Ventnor would require selling a house, but that is manageable. This next roll is mostly safe.

I am weighing whether to trade with player three. Player one is the endgame boss and should not be helped. Player four still wants Tennessee to complete an orange monopoly.

Player one can only build a hotel on Boardwalk because it already has four houses. Park Place needs three houses to reach that threshold, so player one cannot immediately threaten me with a hotel there.

Player one cannot afford to build Park Place to four houses, so the dark blue threat remains at three houses on Park Place and four on Boardwalk. The maximum liquidation from selling all houses and mortgaging the pink properties would yield roughly $300 plus cash, which is insufficient to survive either rent. Mortgaging St. Charles Place, States Avenue, or Virginia Avenue would return about $70, $70, or $80 respectively.

The maximum liquidation from selling all houses and mortgaging the pink properties is roughly $580 to $730. That is still insufficient to survive dark blue rent of $1100 or $1400.

Player four's light blue properties at four houses charge $450 in rent. I already passed them this turn, but they will threaten again on the next orbit. If player four completes an orange monopoly, those properties would cost $550 to $800 each.

Player three's yellow properties at one house pose a moderate threat.

My win condition is simply to be the last player who has not gone bankrupt. I need the other players to land on my pink properties and go broke while I avoid their heavy threats.

With two houses on each pink property, the rent would be about $150 to $200.

A $180 to $200 pink rent would cripple player one by forcing them to sell a dark blue house. Player three would also be hurt, but player four has $457 and would barely notice. Three houses on each pink property would cost $300 total, yet the bank only holds two houses left. I cannot build to three houses on every property.

Player one could use the last two houses to build red properties to two houses each, raising rent to $270–$330. Player four could use them to hotel a light blue property, which would return four houses to the bank and raise rent to $550–$800.

I cannot afford to buy the last two houses, so I will end my turn and preserve my assets. Player three might be a useful trading partner.

Player one has no Get Out of Jail Free card and needs cash to survive. Player three does not need orange properties. I will not break my pink monopoly or sell Tennessee. I might trade a Get Out of Jail Free card for cash.

A Get Out of Jail Free card is more valuable to me than to a player who needs to move. Staying in jail avoids dangerous properties entirely, so I will not trade it cheaply. I am now considering a trade with player four for Tennessee.

Player four could strip light blue houses to fund orange construction. Three houses on orange would cost $550, $600, and $750 each. That is lethal on a high-traffic stretch. I must demand enough cash to prevent them from building.

Player four has $149 surplus after unmortgaging the three orange properties. A $200 sale would leave them with only $257, which is insufficient to unmortgage everything and build. They would be forced to unmortgage two properties and abandon the third, so the orange monopoly would not improve. I would gain roughly $260 in cash. The mortgage value of Tennessee is $90, but completing the orange monopoly is the most valuable asset in the game. Player four may still pay $250 for it despite their recent bankruptcy.

Player four previously rejected a $400 offer for Tennessee. I will not sell that property now. Selling all houses would yield only about $360 in cash, which is insufficient to survive a Connecticut rent of roughly $450.

A $200 cash injection would let me build three houses on two pink properties. That would raise rent to roughly $450–$550 and bankrupt the other players unless they sell buildings. Player four might pay that price for Tennessee, but completing an orange monopoly would create a new threat.

Player one is in a dangerous position. From Connecticut, the orange properties are only seven to ten spaces away, so they will frequently land on them. Player four could use an orange monopoly to attack player one directly. Player one might pay for a Get Out of Jail Free card or to block player four from completing orange.

Player one and player three both oppose an orange monopoly, but neither can afford to pay for it. Player one has only $157 left after buying reds, and player three has $114. The only viable buyer is player four. I will end my turn and wait for a roll that lands on my pink properties.

Player three is safe from my pink properties this turn. Rolling a seven or nine from Water Works would hit Park Place and Boardwalk, both owned by player one with three and four houses respectively. That would likely bankrupt player three immediately.

Player four has roughly $1417 in liquid assets, so a $1400 Boardwalk rent is barely survivable. A $1700 rent would likely bankrupt them. The probability of rolling that exact two is only one in thirty-six.

Player four is mostly safe this turn. Passing GO would add roughly $200, bringing their cash to about $657 after taxes and chance cards. Player one on Connecticut rolls before me. From that position, the pink properties cost about $150 to $200 each.

Player one lands on my pink properties only about 22 percent of the time from Connecticut. If they do, I would collect roughly $150 to $200 and force them into bankruptcy or a house sale. That is the dream scenario. I will not sell houses or trade away the pinks before this roll.

Trading with player four for cash would not help. They would not break their light blue monopoly, and the mortgaged properties they could offer are worthless without the orange set. Player one already paid for the reds after a similar threat, so that tactic is exhausted.

I am weighing whether to propose a trade now. A rejected offer wastes one decision cycle, but the engine will still ask me again for another post-turn action. I am deciding if that risk is worthwhile.

A $250–$350 offer for Tennessee would give me enough cash to build the two remaining houses on my pink properties. Player four could not afford to unmortgage every orange property after paying that price, so they would need to sell houses first.

Player four could liquidate light blue houses to fund orange construction, creating a dangerous threat within one turn. A $400 sale would leave them with only $57, yet they could still strip twelve light blue houses for roughly $600 and build orange. That makes selling Tennessee to player four a losing move. I will not sell it. I am now considering an alternative trade with player three or player one.

Player one would not pay much for a Get Out of Jail Free card, and I need it myself. Player three cannot offer anything useful without completing an incomplete yellow set. I will end my turn and let the pink properties trap the next player.

You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

prompt_messages.content:
You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

your_private_thoughts_last_10.thought: Owe p3 $44 on Atlantic, cash $32, short $12. Only legal sale is 1 house on Virginia (2h vs 1h elsewhere). Half of $100 = $50, covers the debt, leaves ~$38, pinks even at 1/1/1. Do not bankrupt — pinks, TN orange block, reds, and GOOJF are worth far more than $12. Rebuild VA to 2h when rent comes in.

Debt cleared; cash $38, pinks 1/1/1, TN still blocks p4 orange. From Atlantic this roll, only sure death is PP 3h on 11 (2/36, $1100) — no plausible trade covers that. Marvin 1h (roll 3) and Luxury Tax (roll 12) are payable by selling houses. Light blue is behind me. Don't sell houses, don't trade TN/pinks/GOOJF, don't fund p4/p1/p3. Rebuild VA to 2h only after a real cash cushion.

Proposed TN mortgaged to p4 for $400. Cash still $10 until they respond. No other post-turn move helps: can't mortgage/unmortgage/build, selling pink houses only saves the luxury-tax case and guts the only income. Keep GOOJF as a jail shelter. If they accept, bank ~$150 and build pinks toward 2 houses. If they reject, reprice lower before the next roll — PP 3h and BW 4h are still unsurvivable.

On Baltic. Next roll hits p4 light-blue 4h on 3/5/6 (11/36): $450/$500/$550. Liquid with house sales is only $360, so those are fatal. Don't sell houses or build. Don't sell TN to p4 — they profit if I bust on their blues and would get pinks+orange. p1 should pay to complete reds AND to stop p4 inheriting my set. $300 leaves me $510; Conn still needs one house sale. If rejected, drop price or pivot. Keep TN, pinks, GOOJF.

Need ~$190 more to clear p4's $400 blues with houses intact; $240 for Conn $450. $200 covers $400 outright and $450 with one house sale. p1 rejected $300 for buffer; $200+$23 interest leaves them ~$161 plus dark-blue equity. If they refuse, drop to $120 next — even $100 plus selling all 3 houses ($150) survives $450 and keeps pinks unmortgaged. Do not sell TN to p4 (they want me to bust and inherit). Do not build, unmortgage, or sell houses until trades fail. Keep GOOJF and TN orange block.

p1 already knows pink equity saves me from busting, so the inheritance threat is dead. New leverage is credible: if they refuse, sell TN to p4 for cash before p4 rolls. $150 puts me at $360; Oriental/Vermont need 1 house sale, Conn needs 2, pinks stay unmortgaged. Do not sell houses, build, or unmortgage yet. Keep GOOJF and TN. If rejected, next is TN to p4 for ~$350—taking their cash also worsens their Boardwalk hole (4h rent $1700 vs ~$1667 liquidation).

p3 has the TN offer at $150. No build, no house sale, no unmortgage until that resolves — cash has to stay liquid for the Baltic roll into p4's 4-house blues. If they reject, reprice to $100 before ever offering TN to p4. Keep GOOJF and the reds.

Accept my own $150 price. Cash becomes $360, enough to survive p4's 4-house blues from Baltic by selling 1–2 pink houses ($400/$450). Without it, liquid is only $360 including all house sales and those hits bankrupt me into p4, who would inherit pinks, TN (orange), and the reds. Keep TN orange block, pinks, and GOOJF. Do not build or unmortgage before the roll. p1's cheap red monopoly is a later problem.

Built 2/2/2 for $300, cash $60. Even-build legal. p1 on Connecticut rolls before me and hits VA/States/StC on 4/3/1 (6/36) for $180/$150/$150 — that either drops them to ~$7 or forces a house sale, and blocks their $150 red build. If they miss (30/36) they can add one red house; a $250–$300 hit is survivable by selling pink houses, not fatal. BW $1700 and PP $1100 are fatal either way (max liquidation ~$730). Do not unmortgage TN (orange block vs p4) or Penn RR. Do not sell TN to p4. Keep GOOJF and stay in jail if sent. Next goal: 3-house pinks ($450–$500) to crack p4's light blues; only 2 houses left in bank after this.

Cash $60, pinks 2/2/2, TN still blocks p4 orange, GOOJF kept. Only 2 houses left in bank; can't afford another build. Next roll from Penn RR is mostly survivable (red 1h or Ventnor needs one house sale; dark blues and light blues unreachable). p1 on Connecticut hits StC/States/VA on 2/4/5 (~8/36) for ~$150–$200 — that cripples their $157 and their dark-blue houses. Do not sell houses, do not sell TN to p4 (they can strip light blues and build orange), do not fund p1/p3. End turn and let the trap work.

You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

I have $20 and am on Indiana Avenue. I own three properties with one to two houses each, plus one Get Out of Jail Free card. My railroads are mortgaged. My pink monopoly is my main income source. Player 4's light blues at four houses are dangerous. Player 1's dark blues are heavily built and costly. My Tennessee Avenue blocks Player 4 from completing an orange monopoly. I will roll from Indiana Avenue next turn.

Marvin Gardens costs $120 with one house. The next roll lands on Go to Jail. Pacific Avenue and Pennsylvania Railroad are mortgaged, so they cost nothing. The most dangerous roll from Indiana is landing on Park Place with three houses, which would cost $1100.

Selling houses from States Avenue and Virginia Avenue would raise cash to $170. That covers the $130 rent on Ventnor Avenue.

Marvin Gardens costs $120, which two house sales exactly cover. Selling all five houses would raise cash to $270, but that still cannot pay the $1100 rent on Park Place. I am weighing whether to trade, since giving away Tennessee Avenue would let Player 4 complete an orange monopoly and build on it.

I will not sell Tennessee Avenue to Player 4. They already have light blue properties at four houses, so an orange monopoly would be too dangerous. I need to keep my Get Out of Jail Free card for myself.

Player 1 already owns the red monopoly and has no need for my properties. Player 3 already holds the yellow monopoly and is in jail with limited cash, so he cannot pay much. The only viable trade target is Player 4, who wants Tennessee Avenue to complete an orange monopoly. I am considering selling it to Player 4 for $90, though the buyer would inherit the mortgaged status.

Player 1 might buy Tennessee Avenue to block Player 4 from completing an orange monopoly, but he already owns dark blues and reds and may not want to spend cash. Player 3 is too weak to stop Player 4. Selling houses to cover the next roll would weaken my pink income source.

I am weighing specific trade offers to raise cash without giving up my pink monopoly. Player 4 recently paid $1100 in rent and collected $200 passing GO, so they now have $657 and are extremely rich. Player 1 remains the most dangerous opponent with fully upgraded dark blues and reds. My only realistic win condition is to survive as the last non-bankrupt player.

My current two-house holdings on St. Charles Place, States Avenue, and Virginia Avenue are a modest threat. Reaching three houses would raise rent to roughly $450 per property, which could damage Player 4's light blue income.

The housing shortage is severe. Only three houses remain in the bank, and Player 1 has four houses on Boardwalk while Player 4 has four on each light blue. I have five houses total. If I can raise cash to build, I will claim those last three houses and deny them to the other players.

Player 1 might want to build more on the red monopoly or upgrade Boardwalk with a hotel. Selling my Get Out of Jail Free card could raise cash without giving up Tennessee Avenue or my pink properties. Player 3 is in jail with no cards and only $114, so he may be willing to pay for it.

Player 1 already owns the red and dark blue monopolies, so giving him mortgaged Tennessee Avenue would not complete a new set. That makes the trade less appealing than blocking Player 4. I am now weighing which opponent is actually more dangerous: Player 1 with Boardwalk at four houses and Park Place at three, or Player 4 with light blues fully upgraded.

Player 1's next roll from Free Parking will not land on my pink properties. Player 4's roll from Oriental will hit St. Charles Place, States Avenue, and Virginia Avenue.

Player 4's roll from Oriental hits my pink properties on rolls three through five, yielding $50 to $180 in rent. That is manageable with their $657 balance.

My next roll from Indiana Avenue is the real danger. I will likely land on Illinois Avenue, B&O Railroad, Atlantic Avenue, Ventnor Avenue, or Marvin Gardens. Selling houses to cover those expected costs is the immediate priority.

I mapped the exact probability and cash needs for every roll from Indiana Avenue. Ventnor Avenue is the most likely landing, costing $130, followed by Marvin Gardens at $120. The worst outcome is landing on Park Place with three houses, which would cost $1100. I cannot afford to buy North Carolina Avenue with only $20.

I will keep the Get Out of Jail Free card. I can use it to leave jail safely if sent, or stay in jail where I am safe late in the game.

I will not sell houses preemptively. Player 4 can land on my pink properties on rolls three through five, so reducing those holdings now would lower the rent I collect from them. The engine will force debt resolution only when rent is actually due, and I have already handled the current debt. Trading for cash instead would let me avoid selling houses on moderate rent hits while preserving my pink income.

I need roughly $130 to survive the next roll without selling houses. Selling the Get Out of Jail Free card for $50–100 would not cover Ventnor Avenue’s $130 rent, and it would sacrifice my ability to leave jail freely. Mortgaged Pennsylvania Railroad is another option, but Player 4 already owns two railroads and could use a third to collect $100 in rent.

Player 4 could pay $50–80 for mortgaged Pennsylvania Railroad, but that is too little. Player 1 might pay more for Tennessee Avenue, yet an orange monopoly would be lethal. Player 4 has only $657 and would need roughly $484 in unmortgage costs plus house upgrades to build on those properties.

Player 1 could pay up to $247 for Tennessee Avenue, but he needs that cash to survive light blue rent and build on his own monopolies. He cannot reach my pink properties from Free Parking, so the trade would not help him land there immediately.

Player 1 might only pay $50–100 for mortgaged Tennessee Avenue as a blocker, and Player 3 is too weak to offer a good price. The safest path is to end the turn with $20 cash, keep my two-house pink rent intact, and let the engine resolve any debt on my next roll. That preserves the $150–$180 I would collect from Player 4 if they land on my pinks.

Player 4’s expected rent from my pinks is only about $35. I will propose a trade now, since Player 3 is in jail and the next active players are Player 4 and then Player 1.

I am unsure whether a trade proposal resolves immediately or waits for the target player to respond. If Player 4 accepts a trade now, they could unmortgage Tennessee Avenue and upgrade it before I benefit. That would strengthen them too quickly.

I will end the turn. Building, mortgaging, and trading are all impossible or harmful right now. Player 3 is in jail and unlikely to pay well for the Get Out of Jail Free card. Selling houses now would only reduce the rent I collect from Player 4. Trading Tennessee Avenue to Player 4 would be strategically dangerous, and offering it to others for a few dollars is too uncertain.

I cannot trade houses, only properties, cash, or Get Out of Jail Free cards. Player 1 has no urgent need for my card. Player 4 already owns mortgaged Pennsylvania Avenue, so offering them the Pennsylvania Railroad would be pointless.

A $400 sale of mortgaged Tennessee Avenue would leave Player 4 with only $257. Unmortgaging all four orange properties costs roughly $484, so they cannot build on the set immediately. This makes the trade a viable way to raise cash while still blocking an orange monopoly.

Player 4 could sell all four houses on the light blue properties to raise roughly $600. That would cover the remaining $227 needed to unmortgage the orange set and build there immediately. Selling those houses would strip his main weapon, and he may not want to give away his scarce housing stock.

A $350–$450 sale of mortgaged Tennessee Avenue would still leave Player 4 short of the $484 needed to unmortgage the entire orange set, so an orange monopoly would not form immediately. That price could raise enough cash to survive the next roll and perhaps build on my own properties. I am now second-guessing whether to sell it at all, since stripping Player 4 of cash would also deepen his Boardwalk rent hole.

Player 4 cannot pay Boardwalk rent without selling houses. Even after a $400 sale of mortgaged Tennessee Avenue, he would still lack the $1700 needed to cover that debt. He was already bankrupt-bound before this trade. The trade would not improve his ability to pay Boardwalk.

Player 4 cannot pay Boardwalk rent without selling houses. Selling all twelve light blue houses would raise only about $600, leaving a gap of roughly $857 against the $1700 rent. That is more than double the $1100 needed for Pennsylvania Avenue. Extracting $400 from them now would make that shortfall fatal.

Player 4 would likely reject a $400 sale of mortgaged Tennessee Avenue, since that would leave them unable to survive dark blue rent and unable to unmortgage the orange set. A lower offer around $200–$250 might be acceptable instead. I am now weighing whether any reasonable trade exists, or if proposing one would only signal desperation.

A $250 offer for mortgaged Tennessee Avenue would leave Player 4 with roughly $407. That is still too little to survive Pennsylvania Avenue rent, since he would need about $1100 and only has about $1207 after selling houses and mortgaging railroads. The extraction is not large enough to make that rent fatal.

Player 4’s total liquidation is roughly $1617, which covers Pennsylvania Avenue but not Boardwalk. To make Pennsylvania Avenue fatal, his cash after extraction must fall below about $140.

Player 4 would reject a $517 sale of mortgaged Tennessee Avenue because it would bankrupt them on Pennsylvania Avenue. A lower offer around $150–250 would still let them build an orange monopoly later, so that trade is unwise. I will instead propose mortgaged Tennessee Avenue to Player 1 for $100–150, since he has $247 and might accept the cash to block Player 4’s orange path.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. - Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

prompt_messages.content:
You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include Public Message:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Keep the public message token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

Return only a legal tool call and its public_message. Do not include private_thought or a reasoning transcript.

You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.

You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

No other post-turn move helps: can't mortgage/unmortgage/build, selling pink houses only saves the luxury-tax case and guts the only income. Keep GOOJF as a jail shelter. If they accept, bank ~$150 and build pinks toward 2 houses. If they reject, reprice lower before the next roll — PP 3h and BW 4h are still unsurvivable.

On Baltic. Next roll hits p4 light-blue 4h on 3/5/6 (11/36): $450/$500/$550. Liquid with house sales is only $360, so those are fatal. Don't sell houses or build. Don't sell TN to p4 — they profit if I bust on their blues and would get pinks+orange. p1 should pay to complete reds AND to stop p4 inheriting my set. $300 leaves me $510; Conn still needs one house sale. If rejected, drop price or pivot. Keep TN, pinks, GOOJF.

Need ~$190 more to clear p4's $400 blues with houses intact; $240 for Conn $450. $200 covers $400 outright and $450 with one house sale. p1 rejected $300 for buffer; $200+$23 interest leaves them ~$161 plus dark-blue equity. If they refuse, drop to $120 next — even $100 plus selling all 3 houses ($150) survives $450 and keeps pinks unmortgaged. Do not sell TN to p4 (they want me to bust and inherit). Do not build, unmortgage, or sell houses until trades fail. Keep GOOJF and TN orange block.

p1 already knows pink equity saves me from busting, so the inheritance threat is dead. New leverage is credible: if they refuse, sell TN to p4 for cash before p4 rolls. $150 puts me at $360; Oriental/Vermont need 1 house sale, Conn needs 2, pinks stay unmortgaged. Do not sell houses, build, or unmortgage yet. Keep GOOJF and TN. If rejected, next is TN to p4 for ~$350—taking their cash also worsens their Boardwalk hole (4h rent $1700 vs ~$1667 liquidation).

p3 has the TN offer at $150. No build, no house sale, no unmortgage until that resolves — cash has to stay liquid for the Baltic roll into p4's 4-house blues. If they reject, reprice to $100 before ever offering TN to p4. Keep GOOJF and the reds.

Accept my own $150 price. Cash becomes $360, enough to survive p4's 4-house blues from Baltic by selling 1–2 pink houses ($400/$450). Without it, liquid is only $360 including all house sales and those hits bankrupt me into p4, who would inherit pinks, TN (orange), and the reds. Keep TN orange block, pinks, and GOOJF. Do not build or unmortgage before the roll. p1's cheap red monopoly is a later problem.

Built 2/2/2 for $300, cash $60. Even-build legal. p1 on Connecticut rolls before me and hits VA/States/StC on 4/3/1 (6/36) for $180/$150/$150 — that either drops them to ~$7 or forces a house sale, and blocks their $150 red build. If they miss (30/36) they can add one red house; a $250–$300 hit is survivable by selling pink houses, not fatal. BW $1700 and PP $1100 are fatal either way (max liquidation ~$730). Do not unmortgage TN (orange block vs p4) or Penn RR. Do not sell TN to p4. Keep GOOJF and stay in jail if sent. Next goal: 3-house pinks ($450–$500) to crack p4's light blues; only 2 houses left in bank after this.

Cash $60, pinks 2/2/2, TN still blocks p4 orange, GOOJF kept. Only 2 houses left in bank; can't afford another build. Next roll from Penn RR is mostly survivable (red 1h or Ventnor needs one house sale; dark blues and light blues unreachable). p1 on Connecticut hits StC/States/VA on 2/4/5 (~8/36) for ~$150–$200 — that cripples their $157 and their dark-blue houses. Do not sell houses, do not sell TN to p4 (they can strip light blues and build orange), do not fund p1/p3. End turn and let the trap work.

Owe p1 $90, cash $60, short $30. One pink house sale returns $50 and clears it; cash left $20. Sell St. Charles (2h→1h, rent $150→$50) rather than Virginia ($180→$60). Do not bankrupt — 2/2/1 pinks, TN orange block, and GOOJF are worth far more than $30. Rebuild when cash returns. Do not sell TN to p4.

Cash $20, pinks 1/2/2, TN still blocks p4 orange, GOOJF kept. From Indiana only PP on 12 (1/36, $1100) is fatal; rolls 2–6 ($44–$130) are payable by selling houses, 7 is jail, 8–11 are free/mortgaged.
